Cube Illusion

GeometryCoordinatesParadoxes
Game: This drawing can look like a small cube in a corner or a big cube with a corner cut off.
How to play: Move the sliders or drag the corner dot to change the drawing. Press the two highlight buttons to see each shape.
45° · 6 / 3
Look for the math

The same straight lines can be two different solids. Nothing here says which edges are in front, so your eyes settle on one shape — and can switch to the other without the drawing changing at all.

One angle, one grid

The applet draws every line on the same slanted grid. If u is the rounded unit length and t is the tilt, one grid step is (1.6u cos t, u sin t). Vertical edges use only the second part. Because one number t fixes every direction, there is no perspective cue to tell you which way the cube points; the test confirms the step ratio is tan(t) / 1.6 for all ten tilts.

Two solids, the same strokes

The outer outline has six corner points and the inner one has six more; eighteen heavy strokes join them. Read the small hexagon as a cube sitting in a tiled corner, or read the big hexagon as a cube with one corner sliced away. Both readings use exactly those eighteen strokes. This is the trick behind the Necker cube: the ambiguous image has no depth information to prefer one reading. The page's claim that there are at least two ways to see it is checked against every setting: each reading closes into its own hexagon on the very same edges.

What the sliders change

Tilt runs from 15° to 60° in steps of 5°, the big cube from 2 to 10 units, and the small corner from 1 to 10. On every slider move the original sets M = min(N, M), so the small corner cannot outgrow the big cube; this port keeps that quirk. Both grid checkboxes start checked, and the two highlight buttons are a modern aid — the original had no buttons beyond its sliders and checkboxes. When M = N, three of the joining strokes shrink to points in the original too.

Try tilt 15° with a big cube of 10 and a small corner of 2, then click each highlight button without touching the drawing.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
